secondaryKeywords: how to check if a link is nofollow
h1: Dofollow vs nofollow: when to take the link anyway
metaTitle: Dofollow vs Nofollow: When to Take the Link
metaDescription: Dofollow vs nofollow links matter less since 2020, when nofollow became a hint. Here's when to take a nofollow link happily and when to walk away.
answer: A followed link passes ranking signals; a nofollow link tells Google it may ignore them. Since March 2020 nofollow is a hint, not a rule, so Google can count it anyway. Judge a link on whether real people will click it — not on which attribute the publisher's CMS applied by default.
takeaways: "Dofollow" doesn't exist in HTML. Followed is the default; `nofollow` is the markup you add to switch it off.
Since 1 March 2020 Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling and indexing, not a directive. It may follow the link. You don't get told either way.
The better acceptance test is referral traffic. If forty real humans a month click the link, the attribute is a footnote.
A backlink profile that's 95% followed doesn't look strong. It looks bought.

sections.h2: "Dofollow" is not a thing, and that matters
body: There is no `rel="dofollow"` in the HTML spec. There never was. A link is followed by default; `rel="nofollow"` is the markup a publisher adds to stop passing signals. "Dofollow" is jargon SEOs invented to name the absence of an attribute.

That sounds pedantic until you watch what it does to people's judgement. A whole outreach industry has organised itself around a binary that only exists in one direction, and it produces a specific bad habit: checking the attribute first and asking whether the page is any good second. Or never.
The right order is the reverse. Look at the page. Then look at the attribute, if you still care.

In September 2019 Google announced two new link attributes and a change in how it would treat nofollow. From 10 September 2019 the attributes became hints for ranking purposes, and from **1 March 2020** they became hints for crawling and indexing too.

"Hint" means Google may choose to follow a nofollow link and may choose to count it. Google's stated reasoning was that nofollow had become blunt — huge categories of genuinely useful links were being blanket-nofollowed by CMS defaults, and Google was discarding real information about the web.
Two consequences follow, and both are practical.

First, a nofollow link is no longer worth zero. It's worth an unknown amount between zero and something. Nobody outside Google knows which, and no tool reports it. Anyone who tells you a nofollow link definitely passes value, or definitely doesn't, is guessing with confidence.

Second, nofollow stopped being a reliable way to hide a page from Google. If you need something excluded, use `noindex` or block it in robots.txt — see [noindex](/glossary/noindex) for which one applies when.

sections.h2: The three attributes, and when each one applies
body: Publishers now have three markers rather than one. They can be combined — `rel="sponsored nofollow"` is valid and common.

callout.title: The one that carries real risk
callout.body: If you paid for a link — cash, free product, an exchange — it needs `sponsored` or `nofollow`. Undisclosed paid links violate Google's spam policies, and the exposure is on both sides of the transaction. This is the single line in link building worth being boring about.

sections.h2: The better test: would a human click it?
body: Here's the replacement for the attribute check. Stop asking whether a link is followed. Ask whether the page it sits on has readers who might become customers.

The test is measurable, which is what makes it better than a vibe. Take the placement, wait 30 to 90 days, then open GA4 and look at the referral channel for that domain. Sessions, engagement, and — if you're tracking properly — leads.

A nofollow link on a page that sends you forty qualified visitors a month is a customer acquisition channel. Whether Google counts it as a ranking signal is genuinely a secondary question at that point; you're getting paid either way. A followed link on a page nobody reads sends nothing, converts nothing, and gives you a number in a backlink tool.
The test also settles most outreach arguments before they start:
bullets: **Nofollow on a large industry publication your buyers read.** Take it. Immediately. Take it twice.
**Nofollow in a genuine community answer where the question matches your product.** Take it. That's the highest-intent traffic on the internet.

**Followed link on a 'general news' site publishing eight posts a day about insurance, casinos and yoga.** Refuse. The followed attribute is precisely why it's dangerous — see [paid links vs earned links](/compare/paid-links-vs-earned-links).
**Followed link in a footer, a sidebar or a 'partners' block.** Low value at best, a footprint at worst.
**Nofollow in a directory nobody has visited since 2014.** Ignore. Not because of the attribute, because of the nobody.

callout.title: How to check the attribute in four seconds
callout.body: View source, find your link, look for `rel=`. Or `curl -s <url> | grep -i "yourdomain"`. Ahrefs and Semrush both show it as a column on referring-domain exports. You do not need a paid extension for this.

sections.h2: Why an all-dofollow profile is a red flag
body: This is the part that surprises founders who've been buying links, and it's simple arithmetic about how the web behaves.

A brand that genuinely gets talked about accumulates links from places that nofollow by default — press sites with blanket outbound rules, forums, Reddit threads, LinkedIn posts, YouTube descriptions, comment replies, aggregators, syndication feeds. Those are not accidents; they're what real attention looks like when it hits a CMS with defaults.

So a natural profile is mixed. Heavily mixed. Nobody can hand you the correct ratio, because it varies enormously by industry — a B2B SaaS with an active community will look nothing like a jewellery brand — and any specific percentage you see quoted was made up by someone selling something.

But the direction is unambiguous. A profile where nearly every referring domain passes a followed link, with commercially-worded anchor text, did not happen naturally. It happened because someone specified it on an order form. Google's link spam systems are pattern-matchers, and that is a very legible pattern.

The practical version: if you're auditing an inherited profile, a suspiciously clean followed ratio is a stronger signal of purchased links than any domain metric. [Domain authority is a vanity metric](/journal/domain-authority-is-a-vanity-metric) — the shape of the profile isn't.

sections.h2: Nofollow links and getting cited by AI assistants
body: This is the newest reason the attribute matters less than it did, and it's structural rather than speculative.

The `rel` attribute is a link-graph instruction. It tells a crawler something about how to weight an edge between two pages. It says nothing about whether the text on the page is readable, and text is what answer engines consume.

When an AI assistant summarises "best options for X in India", it's working from pages it has ingested. If your brand is named, described accurately and placed in the right category on a page that gets crawled, that's the input. Whether the link next to your name carried `nofollow` does not change what the sentence says about you.

Which flips a long-standing outreach preference. A nofollow mention in a widely-read comparison article on a publication that AI systems read is now plausibly worth more than a followed link on a site with no readers and no reason to be quoted. The same logic runs through [dofollow-obsessed guest posting versus digital PR](/compare/guest-posting-vs-digital-pr) — coverage produces mentions, marketplaces produce attributes.
None of this means links stopped mattering. They matter. It means the attribute was never the thing you were actually buying, and in 2026 it's a smaller fraction of the thing than ever.

callout.title: How we approach link work
callout.body: Last Agency runs SEO from ₹75,000/mo, smaller sites from ₹40,000/mo, ex-GST. We don't buy placements and we don't quote link counts, because a link count isn't an outcome. We freeze your trailing-90-day qualified organic leads on day one and keep working free past 90 days if we haven't beaten it.

versus.verdict: If the link sits on a page your buyers actually read, take it whether it's nofollow or not; only walk away when the page exists purely to host links, in which case the followed attribute is the reason to refuse rather than the reason to accept.

faqs.a: Possibly, directly — since March 2020 Google treats nofollow as a hint and may count it. Certainly, indirectly: referral traffic, brand mentions, and the balance a natural profile needs. What nobody can tell you is how much direct value any individual nofollow link passes, because Google doesn't publish it.

faqs.q: How do I check if a link is dofollow or nofollow?
faqs.a: View the page source, find your link, and look for a `rel` attribute. No `rel` means followed. You can also run `curl -s <url> | grep yourdomain`, or read the attribute column in an Ahrefs or Semrush referring-domains export. No paid tool required.

faqs.q: What's the right ratio of dofollow to nofollow links?
faqs.a: There isn't a published one, and any specific number you're quoted is invented. What's true is directional: a real brand accumulates plenty of nofollow links from forums, press and social platforms, so a profile that's almost entirely followed with commercial anchors reads as purchased rather than earned.

faqs.q: What's the difference between nofollow, sponsored and ugc?
faqs.a: `sponsored` means paid for. `ugc` means a user added it, not the publisher. `nofollow` is the general "don't associate us with this" marker and still works for both. Google treats all three as hints. If you paid for the link, `sponsored` or `nofollow` is not optional.

faqs.q: Should I ask a publisher to remove the nofollow?
faqs.a: Ask once, politely, if the link is genuinely editorial and their CMS applied it by default. Never ask on a paid placement — you'd be requesting an undisclosed paid link, which puts both of you in breach of Google's policies for a signal that may not even move.

faqs.q: Do nofollow links count for AI search visibility?
faqs.a: The attribute is a link-graph instruction; answer engines work from the text on the page. A clear, accurate mention of your brand on a page that gets crawled is the input, regardless of the `rel` value on the link beside it.
